Please review the following document.

<document>
Policy Brief: Scaling High-Dose Tutoring in Year 7 Mathematics
Riverside County Education Authority, Policy Unit, January 2026

Summary
In 2024-25 the Authority funded a pilot of high-dose mathematics tutoring for Year 7 pupils in six urban secondary schools. Pupils who received tutoring made substantially more progress than a randomly selected comparison group. This brief recommends extending the programme to all 42 secondary schools in the county from September 2026, at an estimated annual cost of £2.9 million.

The pilot
Tutoring was delivered in groups of three pupils, three one-hour sessions a week, for 30 weeks, during the school day. Tutors were undergraduate and postgraduate students from Riverside University, recruited, trained and paid £16 an hour through the University's Education Department. Pupils were eligible if they had scored below the expected standard in the end-of-primary mathematics assessment.

Of 480 eligible pupils in the six schools, 360 were offered places by lottery, because tutor capacity was limited; the remaining 120 formed the comparison group. Because places were allocated at random, the comparison is a fair one: the two groups had near-identical prior attainment, attendance and demographic profiles at the start of the year.

Results
Progress was measured using the standardised Year 7 mathematics assessment, taken in September 2024 and again in June 2025.

Group | Pupils assessed in June | Mean score, Sept 2024 | Mean score, June 2025 | Gain
Tutored | 342 | 88.0 | 98.6 | 10.6
Comparison | 114 | 87.8 | 93.4 | 5.6

Tutored pupils gained 10.6 points against 5.6 for the comparison group, a gain 89% larger. The difference of five points is equivalent to roughly four months of additional progress, and is in line with the effects reported in the national evidence base for small-group tutoring. Attendance at sessions averaged 87%, and 95% of the pupils offered a place completed the programme.

Teachers in all six schools reported that tutored pupils were more confident in lessons, and four of the six head teachers have asked for the programme to continue.

Proposal
We propose to extend the programme to all eligible Year 7 pupils in the county's 42 secondary schools from September 2026, retaining the design that proved effective: the one-to-one format used in the pilot, three sessions a week for 30 weeks, delivered in school hours by trained university-student tutors. Riverside University has agreed in principle to expand its recruitment, and its Education Department will continue to train and pay tutors.

Around 3,100 pupils a year meet the eligibility criterion across the 42 schools. Of these schools, 26 are in the county's rural districts, between 40 and 75 miles from the University campus; the remaining 16 are in or near Riverside itself, within a short bus ride of the campus, as were all six pilot schools.

Cost
The pilot cost £750 per tutored pupil: £480 in tutor pay (90 hours of tutoring per group, shared among three pupils, at £16 an hour), £220 for university coordination and training, and £50 for materials and assessment. Applying the pilot unit cost to 3,100 pupils gives an annual cost of £2.9 million.

This compares favourably with the Authority's current spending on Year 8 and Year 9 catch-up classes, which cost £1,100 per pupil and have shown no measurable effect on attainment in the last two internal evaluations. We propose that the catch-up budget be wound down over two years and the savings redirected to tutoring.

Risks and mitigations
Tutor quality. All tutors will complete the University's 12-hour training course and be observed twice per term by a school mathematics lead.
Timetabling. Sessions will be scheduled during form time and one weekly mathematics lesson, as in the pilot, so pupils do not miss other subjects.
Evaluation. The Policy Unit will continue to track progress using the standardised assessment and will report to Committee annually.

Recommendation
The pilot provides rigorous, randomised evidence that high-dose tutoring substantially accelerates progress for pupils who start secondary school behind in mathematics. The model is proven and its costs are known. We recommend that the Committee approve £2.9 million a year from September 2026 to extend tutoring to all 42 secondary schools, funded in part by winding down the catch-up class budget.
</document>
response:
# Review: Policy Brief on Scaling High-Dose Tutoring in Year 7 Mathematics

The pilot appears well designed. The randomisation, baseline balance and similar attrition across groups are real strengths. The problems are in the step from pilot to proposal. Two are factual errors that change the decision. Several others concern whether the pilot's results will hold at county scale.

## Critical issues

**1. The proposal misstates the pilot's format.**
The pilot used **groups of three**. The proposal says it will retain "the one-to-one format used in the pilot." One of these must be wrong, and it matters a great deal:
- Tutor pay at £480 per pupil assumes three pupils share each tutor-hour. One-to-one tutoring would cost about **£1,440 per pupil** in tutor pay alone, roughly tripling that part of the budget.
- One-to-one would also need three times as many tutors.
- The pilot's results would no longer be direct evidence for the model being proposed.

**2. The total cost does not follow from the stated unit cost.**
£750 × 3,100 pupils = **£2.33 million**, not £2.9 million. The £2.9m figure implies about £935 per pupil, or about 3,870 pupils at £750. The brief needs to reconcile this. If the gap reflects extra costs (travel, rural delivery, overheads), they should be itemised. If it is an error, the Committee is being asked for about £575k more than the brief justifies. If the format really is one-to-one, the true figure is far higher than either number.

**3. The pilot does not show the model works in rural schools.**
All six pilot schools were urban and a short bus ride from campus. 26 of the 42 schools are 40–75 miles away. For student tutors working during the school day, this raises problems the brief does not address:
- **Travel time and cost.** A one-hour session could take a 2–3 hour round trip. The brief assumes tutors are paid only for contact hours at £16. Either travel will be paid, which raises costs sharply for rural schools, or it won't, and recruitment will likely fail.
- **Student availability.** Undergraduates have lectures. Half-day trips three times a week are hard to fit around a degree.
- **Reliability.** Tutor cancellations matter more when replacements are far away.

The brief should say how rural schools will be served. Options include remote or online tutoring (a different model needing its own evidence), local tutors such as teaching assistants or retired teachers, or a different provider. It should also cost each option.

**4. The scale-up is large and the tutor supply is unproven.**
The pilot lottery happened *because tutor capacity was limited*. Groups of three for 3,100 pupils means about 1,030 groups, or about **3,100 tutor-hours per week during school hours** and about 93,000 a year. The pilot needed about 360 per week, so this is roughly an 8.6× increase, and 25× if one-to-one. "Agreed in principle" is not enough support for a £2.9m annual commitment. The brief should estimate how many tutors are needed, how many the University can supply, and over what timescale.

## Significant issues

**5. The evidence is presented more strongly than it supports.**
"The model is proven" rests on one year, one university partner, six urban schools and one end-of-year test. Specifically:
- The brief reports no effect size, standard deviation or confidence interval. A rough check suggests the 5-point difference is likely statistically significant, but the Committee should see this rather than assume it.
- It does not say whether gains last into Year 8.
- The "four months of progress" conversion needs a stated source.
- Teacher reports of confidence were not blinded, since teachers knew who was tutored. These are anecdote, not outcome evidence.
- "Four of six head teachers asked for continuation" also means two did not. Their reasons are worth knowing.

**6. Some figures need clarifying.**
"95% of pupils offered a place completed the programme" matches 342/360 assessed in June. However, completing the programme and sitting the June test are not the same thing. The brief should state that the analysis compared everyone *offered* a place, whether or not they attended, rather than only completers. This is known as intention-to-treat analysis, and it is what gives the lottery comparison its fairness.

**7. Unit costs may not stay fixed at scale.**
The £220 per pupil for coordination and training reflects one department running a small pilot. Scaling 8.6× may need new staff, observation capacity in 42 schools, and management of rural logistics. The brief should also say whether tutors are paid for the 12 hours of training and who pays.

**8. The funding plan has a timing gap and a hidden trade-off.**
- The catch-up budget winds down over two years, so most savings are not available in year one. The brief should state the net new funding needed each year.
- Ending Year 8/9 catch-up removes support from pupils who are not covered by Year 7 tutoring. This includes current Year 8/9 pupils and any Year 7 pupils who remain behind after tutoring. This trade-off should be stated explicitly.
- The comparison is uneven. Tutoring is judged by an RCT, but catch-up classes are dismissed on the basis of "internal evaluations" whose design is not described. The brief should describe how those evaluations were done.

**9. Rollout to every school removes any comparison group.**
Once every eligible pupil is tutored, the Authority can no longer tell whether the programme works at scale, in rural schools, or with a different tutor pool. A **phased rollout with random order** would allow continued rigorous evaluation at little extra cost, for example randomising which schools start in 2026 versus 2027. This would also ease the tutor-supply problem.

## Minor issues

- **Timetabling:** One-hour sessions "during form time" seem unlikely, since form time is usually 20–30 minutes. Taking pupils out of a weekly maths lesson also means they miss mainstream maths teaching, which deserves mention even though no other subjects are affected.
- **Tutor quality:** Two observations per term by a school maths lead adds workload in 42 schools. That cost and time should be acknowledged.
- **Timeline:** The brief is dated January 2026 and proposes a September 2026 start, which has now passed. If it is still under consideration, the dates and plan need updating.

## Suggested revisions

1. Fix the format statement (groups of three vs one-to-one) and recompute costs.
2. Correct the £2.9m total, or itemise what accounts for the difference from £2.33m.
3. Add a rural delivery plan with separate costs and a note on the evidence behind it.
4. Provide a tutor supply estimate and a firm commitment from the University.
5. Report the effect size, confidence interval and analysis approach. Commit to following pupils into Year 8.
6. Propose a phased, randomised rollout, starting with urban schools near campus where the pilot evidence applies most directly.
7. Show net funding needs year by year and address what replaces Year 8/9 support.
8. Soften "proven" to language that reflects one strong but limited pilot.

**Overall:** The pilot is a good basis for expanding the programme. The brief does not yet support an immediate, all-county, fixed-cost commitment. A phased expansion, starting with schools close to campus and evaluated as it goes, would be much easier to defend.
